utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief of your present witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Gojanovic into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I inform the parties that immediately after yesterday's morning, session through The Victims and Witness Section, the witness was informed, was instructed that he should not speak with anyone about his testimony, whether already given or still to be given. I failed to do that at the end of the session, but I immediately corrected myself after the session. Do we have already any idea about how much time cross-examination would take, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the risk of being accused of being vague, it will take several hours, Your Honour, and I'm not confident that we will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other parties? Yes, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I estimate approximately 20 to 30 minute, probably 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic or Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I probably will have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Gojanovic. I'd like to remind you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony; that is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Mahindaratne will now continue the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gojanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 13 of your 1995 [sic] statement, the first statement you gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have it on the screen. Now Exhibit P194, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1995 is 2005, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I always make that mistake. I'm sorry, Mr. President. 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13, you referred to entering Kistanje and seeing Croatian military present. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were these just individual soldiers coming into the area in a sporadic fashion, or were they structured units moving through the process of the military operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would confirm that those were military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did those units seem to have, from what you could observe, the other necessary elements available to military units such as logistics, communication, commanders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not observe that, because if I look back, I must have gone through Kistanje very fast. I didn't notice their exact disposition, their logistics, anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. That's all right. In that same paragraph further down, you refer to learning about the Kistanje post office being burned by the SIS men from the 113th Brigade. Now, can you explain us to what "SIS" stands for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, from my military knowledge, "SIS" is the security service within the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did -- from what you know, did all brigades have SIS units attached to them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, I suppose that all brigades had within them an organisation, a unit, connected to the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I just take you to paragraph 20 of this statement. And further down, towards the latter part of the paragraph, you say: "I must add that members of the 113th Brigade were looting and taking looted property back to Sibenik on the transport provided by the military or, in some cases, even in their own vehicles." Now, how did you know this? What is the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw, while I was there in Donji Srb, that members of - I can't say exactly 113th Brigade, as it says in this statement of 2005 - but I generally saw that soldiers placed in private cars certain items, drove them away somewhere; and, on the other hand, I also saw drivers, military drivers who normally transported troops, put other property in their military vehicles and drove them away to the point where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was this something you saw once in a while, or did you see such things regularly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, I saw such things happen in the course of one day; but later on I wouldn't have been able to see such things because I was deployed closer to the forest. I was in an environment where there was a lot of smoke, a wooded area, areas where houses are scattered across a distance. So I wouldn't have been able to observe what happened on the main road because I was quite far from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why was there a lot of smoke?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time we arrived at Donji Srb, there was a large concentration of smoke from the fires that engulfed the woods, the barns, the houses. But the area of Donji Srb, unlike - and local people will understand this - unlike the Netherlands where houses are close to one another in a plain, in this area, houses are scattered over a large area. You can't see where the smoke is coming from, and every soldier took a long time to get rid of that smoke, which simply infiltrated our nostrils, or bodies, or brains almost.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you referred to looted goods being transported on what you referred to as transport provided by the military or military transporters. Now were these transporters, transporting systems, carried out in an organised fashion in convoys, or were they carried out in an ad hoc manner? Can I give some idea as to how the transporting took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the statement says "on the transport provided by the military or, in some cases, even in their own vehicles," I'm not sure that is the same as saying transport systems provided for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please rephrase in such a way that it literally reflects what is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, you refer to looted goods being transported, and let me quote you verbatim, "on the transport provided by the military." Now, could you give the Trial Chamber an idea as to what exactly -- what vehicles are these and how are they organised. Do they travel in convoys, or do they travel in an ad hoc manner?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said very clearly, in my last statement, too, I believe, that I was talking about military vehicles. You could say buses from local transport companies that had been commandeered by the army, but one should also mention that these buses that transported troops to the area of Donji Srb were civilian by civilian drivers, civilian drivers who were normally employed by civilian forwarding and transport companies but were given the assignment to drive those troops in that assignment. So I cannot say that all of them were military vehicles; but as far as buses are concerned, I can tell you that coming to or leaving a particular area in the field, these buses were put in a motorcade, in a convoy, and these convoys were not particularly long, as far as the 113th Brigade was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let me take you, Mr. Gojanovic, to paragraph 23. And there you say, with reference to looting: "There was even an unofficial authorisation to take war booty when the Croatian army liberated an area." I'm sorry. Let me take you back one sentence before that. You say: "At no time did the political affairs department or SIS issue instructions that the looting, destruction, and killings must stop. There was even an unofficial authorisation to take war booty when the Croatian army liberated an area. This was valid for about three days, and so it was believed to be acceptable to loot property and to consider it as war booty. After three days, the international community had Operation Oluja under close scrutiny, but by then it was more difficult to stop it happening." Can you tell the Court as to how you -- what is the basis of your knowledge that there was an unauthorised approval, unofficial authorisation to take property?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after four years of war, in which certain areas in Croatia had been constantly under the pressure of shelling by, we can say, Krajina soldiers, in that sense it is quite certain that a feeling of bitterness prevailed among the people. And in the course of those four years, everybody wished that this area, which we call Krajina here and which is actually a normal, regular part of the Republic of Croatia, everybody wished that this area would be recovered to the sovereignty of Croatia. After those four years, the troops, after breaking through the first line of defence in the Operation Storm, were overwhelmed by a feeling of euphoria once they stepped on to this territory that Croatia had not under its control for four years. And in those circumstances, it was rather difficult to demand from Croatian soldiers to obey the normal order that is to be expected in -- in regular circumstances, in the regular functioning of the army. It was absolutely not sufficient to warn each individual soldiers -- each individual soldier to refrain from picking up an item or two from a house. It was even sort of acceptable. However, in the end, these things were not really needed, so soldiers eventually left these things they didn't need in the houses where they found them. And as time went on, they realised how redundant all that was, how unnecessary. All this was tolerated and there was some sort of understanding towards those soldiers; and, again, not every soldier could be under the control of his command at every moment. I'm not saying that these things were approved, but it was -- there was a feeling that it was kind of justified at first. At that time, I wasn't quite sure whether it was because of the international community's presence or for some other reason; but, eventually, it turned out that it took those three days for the international community to grapple with this Operation Storm and to take it under control. And, anyway, during those three days, it was felt that this theft was normal and tolerable after those four years of constant shelling. From the human point of view, it was some sort of justification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that long answer, Mr. Gojanovic. Let me take you to paragraph 16 of your statement, P194 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask, Ms. Mahindaratne, one question in between.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, you're explaining what happened and that it was felt as more or less justified during a couple of days. About the scale, did it happen on a scale that could have escaped anyone's eye of those who were present in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who do you mean, Your Honour? Those who were present; the army, in general; the troops; or everyone who was present in that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, everyone who was present. You were there as a soldier. There may have been remaining inhabitants. Was it at a scale that you say it could not, or could it have escaped anyone's eye when it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was, indeed, on a scale that it had to be noticed. It must have been noticed by anyone who was there in the field. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is also -- you're now referring to those first three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, could you please look at paragraph 16 of your statement, where you refer an incident where you prevented --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Paragraph 16 of your statement. In that, I'm referring to that incident where you prevented some fellow soldiers from causing harm to women. And in relation to that incident, you state that while you were in Zrmanja, you heard talk among soldiers that some of your colleagues had gone off to rape some women, and then you go on to say that none of the commanders of the 113th Brigade were perturbed about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say "none of the commanders," whom are you referring to? I'm not asking for names. I'm asking whether they are platoon commanders; company commanders; or brigade commander, himself.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were platoon commanders gathered, more or less, in one house in the centre of Zrmanja, trying to organise this time of rest before moving on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you described how you prevented that incident using your personal authority. Can you tell Court as to what was the personal authority you had which enabled you to exercise such control over your fellow soldiers? And if you could, perhaps keep your response short, Mr. Gojanovic. We are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be very specific. Before I was mobilised into the 113th Brigade, I was a member of the 4th Split Brigade; and before I was -- after I was demobed from the 4th Split Brigade, I retained my uniform and other equipment that I continued to use later on in Operation Storm. According to the rules of service, as a member of the 113th Brigade, I had a rather special uniform with some insignia taken over from the 4th Split Brigade. I mean, the badge on the chest, and an indication that would tell other soldiers that I had experience in a professional brigade that enjoyed respect in the eyes of the 113th Brigade. I also had personal authority because I had come to that house to check the situation, and the soldiers could see that I had been in the 4th Split Brigade. It must have influenced them in a positive way, since they eventually left and things returned, more or less, to normal. Was I brief enough in my answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gojanovic. Now, in paragraph 17, you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me take you to paragraph 20, since we are running out of time, Mr. Gojanovic. You recall an incident where Commander Kotlar arrived in a vehicle and shouted at the troops, telling them not to loot or torch; and then you go on to say that you did not think that the troops may have taken that seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could read it verbatim, it doesn't say he "did not think." It says, "I'm not sure they took him seriously."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I said, Mr. President: "... then you go on to say that did you not think that the troops ..." Well, I could just say he was not sure. It is about the same, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "I recall that Commander Kotlar visited the area of Donji Srb on one occasion in his four-wheel drive vehicle and shouted at the troops, telling them not to loot or torch. Although, I'm not sure they took him seriously." Now whom are referring to as Commander Kotlar?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Danijel Kotlar was then-commander of the 113th Brigade, and the stage in Donji Srb was where soldiers were just beginning to occupy their temporary accommodation and many things were yet unknown. Danijel Kotlar was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to get his identify. I'm sorry. We are returning out of time? The next question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find that in paragraph 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you, Mr. Gojanovic. When Commander Kotlar arrived, was there looting and burning in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the immediate vicinity, there certainly was no burning or looting, at least not that could be observed from this place. But as I said a little earlier, there was smoke everywhere. So it could be concluded that certain buildings were actually burning at the time, houses or some other buildings. But it is certain that from the area where we were, we could not observe that houses were set on fire or that looting was being done. So had you to come a lit closer to actually establish that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 14 of the proofing note, P196, I'm referring to the other document. Not this document, Mr. Gojanovic. I'm referring to the proofing note, Mr. Gojanovic, P196, paragraph 14. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the corrections or?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the last correction dated 14th May 2008. Yes. Paragraph 14 you, say that: "The burning and looting was such that it was obvious to everybody around what was going on."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, beyond that incident where Commander Kotlar shouted from the vehicle not to loot and burn, during the period, 4th August to the time you were demobilised, did you or are you aware of any orders being issued to stop the looting and destruction?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no. However, I do remember that there were instructions, because this was the first time that I also told the members of my -- that I met the members of my platoon that I was supposed to with from the very start. So the only instruction was that we shouldn't go, venture out too far from the house where we were stationed, so that we would not bring ourselves into danger. So these were instructions relating to security measures, and we also had information about where the Main Staff was. This was really just so we would have information as to the structure in the area, because after the, what you called, incident, the matters began to ease up, and the army was actually put up in houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say instructions regarding -- relating to security measures, is that security measures for the troops or for others?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, this dealt with the structure of or the organisation of the men in the field, and these were instructions for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And just to clarify that, when I said "security for the soldiers," security of the soldiers or of others? That's what I meant to ask you. When I say "security of the soldiers," that they will not expose themselves to any threat or the safety of others outside the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to be as specific as I can. The verbal instruction had to do with the security of the men, the soldiers, for a very special reason, because we didn't know who was where in that area and whether there were any enemy troops there, still, that could threaten the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: One last question -- last two questions, actually, Mr. Gojanovic. In paragraph 25 of your statement, I'm talking about original statement, your first statement. You refer to -- you refer to the Varivode killings, and you refer to - I'm taking you right down toward the end of that paragraph - where you say: "All responsibility from the armed forces ..." -- I'm sorry. Let me go back a sentence. "After the crime, VONS found out about the TV footage, and so they so they decided to cover it up and remove all responsibility from the armed forces by demobilising two or three of the accused, to make it appear that they were not serving members of the Croatian army when the alleged crime took place." Now first question: What is "VONS"? And if you could respond to me with a quick answer. What does "VONS" stand for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence and National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how did you know about the demobilisation of the accused in the Varivode case? What was the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the last question that you're going to put?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One last. All right. Well, let me put it this way: From documents that I collected as the president of the society for years, and which I handed over to the Prosecution, I think in 2003, when we requested to have a meeting with the Chief Prosecutor, who, at that time, was Carla Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think you already answered the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, we have not been produced any documents from the Office of the Prosecutor produced by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in fact, we do have some documents relating to the incident; but at this stage, I'm not in a position to say if, in fact, the source of those documents is this witness or if it was another person who was connected to this witness. So, in relation to the ISU searches, those documents did not come up with regard to this witness; but, however, all documents have been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, when you say "produced by this witness," that's ambiguous language, isn't it? You can produce a document in two ways, either by drafting a document, making a document, and the other one is to hand it over to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, regardless of whether it was prepared by him or they were prepared by someone else and turned over by him, we have no information that this witness gave any documents to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution under an obligation to tell you where, from every document, where they collected it from, from whom they got it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, particularly if a witness who is coming to testify in court, and then is going to be asked on direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He wasn't asked. He spontaneously came up with -- the question was just: How do you know? He was not asked about documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He was not asked about documents. He was asked for his basis of knowledge, which turns out to be documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, if she is going to ask him his basis of knowledge of the underlying statement which turn out to be documents, that we don't know what those documents are and, therefore, how are we supposed to cross-examine on his basis of knowledge, given that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although, these document were disclosed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think what documents she is referring to. We have 10.000 documents produced, if not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see to what extent it bothers you and to what extent -- if perhaps during the next break, first of all, Ms. Mahindaratne explains to you what these documents are and why she didn't draw your attention to it, because that seems to be a major concern. It's not a matter of disclosure, but rather why you were not informed that these documents, apparently relevant in relation to this witness, that we were not informed about having received these documents. And, of course, the other question, Ms. Mahindaratne, would be that if you were aware, let's just for arguments sake assume that, that the knowledge of this witness was based on these documents, then one could wonder why, what appears in his statement just to be fake knowledge, why, if there is a clear documentary basis for this, and if you aware of that, why not present that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I was not aware. In fact, it was Mr. Misetic who raised it; and, in fact, Mr. Tieger has had discussions about this matter with Mr. Misetic. We have informed Mr. Misetic as to exactly where we stand. We were not aware that this witness handed over any documents to the OTP, but there is another witness who has handed over material. So there is no connection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see, because, at this moment, it is still a little bit vague to me what you knew, what you should have known, perhaps. There apparently have been conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is different than what I was represented. I was told this morning that there was nothing found in the search. I did raise an issue last night, and I was told there is nothing in the records thus far in the searches by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. There is nothing found. What, in fact, was pointed out is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following. Apparently, a new element arises at this moment, that you first take the opportunity during the next break, perhaps with Mr. Tieger and you, Ms. Mahindaratne, and that you speak with Mr. Misetic, preferably in the presence of other counsel as well, so they don't miss any information, that you see after this discussion what remains as a matter perhaps to be dealt with by this Chamber, and then we will be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That includes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Misetic, you can stand up right away again, at least if it is you who is it the first one to cross-examine the witness. You asked whether it was the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Gojanovic, if there is anything that you would like to add to your statement, that's fine. If there is any anything you would like to add --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is. There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please add what you wish to add. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say something about this last issue: The Varivode case, and the Varivode Zrmanja, Varivode Gosici. I have to clarify a specific role I had before this Court because I am here as a person, so Vladimir Gojanovic; but also as a long-term member of my organisation which was the Croatian Society --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the name of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Croatian Association of Demobilised Participants of the Homeland War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, before you continue, I take it that your role in that organisation will be dealt with during cross-examination, unless there's something spectacular new. But if you would like explain your role in that organisation, I take it that you will have an ample opportunity during cross-examination to give all kinds of details Mr. Misetic or other Defence counsel might ask you about. If at the very end there is still information you think this Chamber should be aware of in this respect, you will have an opportunity to tell us. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, but I still wanted to add something. However, if it is certain that the Defence will also question me in relation to that case, it is absolutely my intention that, in keeping with the oath that I gave, I protect the truth and to provide a statement that is as thorough as possible, so that the final decision in this case is fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one expects you to do anything else than to firmly stick to the solemn declaration you've given. Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina, and he will now cross-examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gojanovic. Let me start by following-up with a question on an answer you recently gave, concerning the authority you enjoyed in the 113th Brigade as a result of your participation earlier in the 4th Guards Brigade. Would you say that you were conspicuous to the other members of the 113th as a result of your prior affiliations with the 4th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I wouldn't say that. I would rather say that that role was confirmed as a very valuable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we misunderstood each other. Because of your prior affiliations in the 4th Guards Brigade, did the other members of the 113th take particular notice of you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was conspicuous because I did not have the same insignia and because the 4th Guards Brigade is still one of the most respected Brigades in the homeland war; and in that sense, there was a certain respect, not for me as an individual because I wore that uniform, but also indirectly out of respect for the 4th Split Brigade in the Homeland war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that answer. I'm going to take some time with you now, Mr. Gojanovic. I noted in your statement that there are a lot of names that are not in your statement. So I'd like to take several minutes now with you to get some names of some of the individuals that we're talking about in your statement. So if you could start off by telling us who was -- give us the name of your squad commander when you started on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the squad commander, the squad where I was, was Jozo Marinovic; the commander of the 113th Sibenik Brigade was Danijel Kotlar; and, my platoon commander, I don't think I know his name and I don't think I will ever learn it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was my next question. So you don't know the name of your platoon commander. What about your company commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. The witness has already, at paragraph 26, said that he cannot recall the name of the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say the question was superfluous and then taking time to explain what is superfluous is superfluous as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it stricken now the question or perhaps he recollects today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes. But I would not encourage the parties to ask the witness whatever he said he didn't remember at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you don't know your platoon commander; you don't know your company commander; you don't know your battalion commander; and your brigade commander was Mr. Kotlar. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Misetic, as a matter of fact, you asked: "Is it stricken now the question?" As a matter of fact, I did not intend to prevent the witness from giving an answer to your question. I was just commenting on a rather useless intervention on what I thought might be a superfluous question, but we never know. I agree with you; and as I said before, I do not encourage the parties to put all the questions to the witness when he earlier in the statement said they don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not for you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your response was in English. What you said, you said in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I usually speak English here, so I do not exactly know what -- did you not receive translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did not receive translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a fair objection. It is not an objection against the question. Then, Mr. Misetic, perhaps you put the question that was finally not answered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was Jozo Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the name you gave -- I asked you -- my first question was: Who was your squad commander? You said it was Jozo Marinovic. So was Jozo Marinovic your battalion commander or your squad commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was the battalion commander, as far as I can recall. And as for information, let's clarify that so we avoid any superfluous questions, I don't remember who the squad commander was or who the company commander was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were right, Mr. Misetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 7 of your statement, you say: "Some lower-level commanders of the 2nd Battalion decided we had to launch an attack using volunteers." Who are the lower-level commanders you're referring to, by name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but I had some difficulty with my headset and I did not follow. I couldn't follow which paragraph and which statement the question related to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 of the 2005 statement, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What are the names of the lower-level commanders of the 2nd Battalion that you refer to there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know, that's four sure. After all this time that has elapsed and the distance, you also have to bear in mind that I had only recently joined the 113th Brigade where I came from the 4th Guards, and I didn't really know the people. So this was a major difficulty also in recognizing the people who were commanders and those who weren't, during the action itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, you answered that question in five words, and then you explained why you didn't know. There's no need to do that. We accept if you do not know. If there's any doubt about the reasons, Mr. Misetic will ask you about it. So if he asks "Do you know?", just simply say that you don't remember their names. Then if there is any need for a follow-up, Mr. Misetic will not fail to give that follow-up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, sir, towards the bottom of page 4, it says: "We gathered on a side road that was in an elevated position; and with the use of a tank that had joined us, we went towards Sonkovici. The tank commander was considered our commander for this mission." What is the name of the tank commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The tank commander's nickname was "Judge" Sudac. I don't know exactly what his name was, but he was an experienced fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So Sudac's name be Radoslav Juricev?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes. From Vodice, Juricev, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Earlier on in that paragraph, you say: "Since our initial attack was not successful, the following day, I was one of ten volunteers that infiltrated enemy lines." Can you give us the names of some or all of the ten volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of their last name was Zafranovic and I know one of them, but that is not sufficient for your information. I cannot remember all the names of all the volunteers who volunteered for this, and that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is Zafranovic's name "Davor"? Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know the man, but I don't know if his name is Davor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph on the next page, in English version, it says: "One part of my team captured the UNPROFOR peacekeepers." Can you identify any of the individuals who were part of your team who captured the UNPROFOR peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A little lower down in that same paragraph, it says: "Another part of my group, the part I was in with the tank, attacked and destroyed the machine-gun post from the left." Can you identify any or all of the other members of that part of the group?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. It was too many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... second sentence: "I climbed on top of a tank with about six other soldiers." Can you name any or all of these six other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, expect the tank commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that is the man you identified earlier as "Sudac." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same paragraph, second-to-last sentence: "Because the 113th had moved slower than was necessary, after the success of taking Djevrska, seven volunteers, including myself, spent one night in the town. The volunteers included three conscripts. During that night, we searched the whole of the town." Can you identify any or all of the seven volunteers that spent the night in the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one nicknamed "Mis," Mouse; but I don't know their name, their real names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 9, in the middle of the paragraph: "The person who came behind me, the one on the motorcycle from the 113th Brigade, then shot and killed one of the surrendered soldiers in front of me." Then the last sentence says: "I do not know the name of the soldier who killed the Krajina soldier, but I know he is very young and I have not seen him for a very long time, even though he also lives in Sibenik."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This statement is from 2005, sir. Since 2005, has our memory been refreshed as to the identity of the soldier who killed the prisoner of war, according to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It has been a very, very long time since I last heard from him or saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you do know that he lives in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that he lives in Sibenik, because from the time of the incident, I saw him only twice. But after a number of years, I haven't seen him again, so I'm no longer sure whether he lives in Sibenik or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on a previous anticipate you gave. You identified one of the seven in Djevrska as being nicknamed "Mis." Does the name Josip Elez mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10, this is now the story of the young soldiers trying to burn down the house with the women in it. Can you identify, by name, any of the very young soldiers of the 113th Brigade who were engaging in this conduct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Further on in the paragraph : "Together with another very good soldier, a citizen of Serbian ethnicity, who was in our army, I began checking the military warehouse, but we found no other enemy soldiers." What is the name of "this soldier of Serbian ethnicity who was in our army"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his last name was Despot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this, but let me take you back to paragraph 6. I forgot to ask you about this. In paragraph 6, last sentence: "One of my colleagues was hit by a bullet and killed. Another was wounded. I went with two other soldiers with the wounded soldier and pulled him on a collapsed tent back towards a house in the direction of Pavasovici." First, can you identify, by name, the killed soldier?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify, by name, the wounded soldier?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could recognise him if I saw him, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the two other soldiers whom you went with to the wounded soldier?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would not have asked this question if you would not have addressed the matter of the other very good soldier. Mr. Misetic asked you about who it was, the other very good soldier, where you said you began checking the military warehouse but found no other enemy soldiers. In the next line, it reads: "We did find military equipment but not soldiers." Could you tell me what kind of military equipment you found in that warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about the military depot. There were certain armoured vehicles that were no longer fit for use, armoured military vehicles, intended for transportation of troops. I also recall there were some elements of cannons; but all in all, the amount of weaponry in the depot was not as high as it used to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Following up on that question, you identified this good soldier as last name Despot. Do you know if his first name is Ratko?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what battalion he was a part of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, first sentence: "Later, I think it was the same day of August 1995" -- "of 6 August 1995, our same group of seven volunteers went through Kistanje." Can you tell us the names of any or all of the seven volunteers whom you went through Kistanje with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the one I mentioned already nicknamed "Mis," Mouse, I can't recall any other names. I'm not even sure whether Despot was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same paragraph, towards the middle, I think you were asked this question by the Prosecutor: "I later learned from someone in the 142nd Brigade that the SIS men from the 113th Brigade torched the post office in Kistanje which was a ridiculous act." Who was the individual from the 142nd Brigade that told you this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he was, and I have to say that I'm not even sure whether he was a member of the 142nd Brigade. I had inferred that he was from the Zadar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, second sentence: "We had rejoined our unit of the 113th, and the people around me were different and I was not part of my original platoon. Can you identify, by name, any of the individuals whom you describe as "the people around me" in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, there were two or three platoons. I knew one person under the last name of Bavos [phoen], but I'm not sure if he was in my platoon. I think he was in one of the other platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 16, third sentences: "I heard talk amongst those soldiers that some of their colleagues had gone off to rape some women." Can you identify, by name, the soldiers who were talking about their colleagues going off to rape some women?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify, by name -- let me take a step back. On questioning from the Prosecutor this morning, you were asked about who the commanders are in the next sentence, which is: "None of the commanders of the 113th Brigade seemed to be at all perturbed by this." And your answer was that this was a reference to platoon commanders. My question is: Please identify, by name, these platoon commanders.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot identify them after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Further on down in that paragraph. "I went to the house where the mother and daughter were located; and on entering, I saw three or four soldiers, one of whom I knew, and who were members of the 113th Brigade." Can you, first, identify for us the soldier whom you say in your statement you knew?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him by sight, but I don't know his first name, last name, or nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, later on in that same statement, towards the bottom of this paragraph on page 10, you say: "I know who one of the soldiers was, but I don't wish to mention his name." Are you not giving us his name because you don't recall or because you don't want to tell us who it is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think this was misinterpreted. I know the man by sight. I don't know his name. Even now, with the best intentions, I cannot tell you his name. That's the only answer I can offer. But it's certainly not true that I don't wish to identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going back up to that previous sentence about seeing the three or four soldiers, I asked you about the one you say in your statement that you knew. What about the other two or three soldiers, do you know them by name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you this question and, I ask you to answer it "yes" or "no," without giving a name. Do you know the names of either of the two women you say were about to be raped? Yes or no, no names, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same paragraph, on page 11 of the English. "There were other members of the 113th Brigade who I'd heard were going to rape the woman; although, it wasn't as obvious as in the first house." Can you identify, by name, whom you heard this information from?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Next sentence: "Again, I argued with them and told them that I would kill them if they tried to do anything stupid to the women." Can you identify by name who it is you argued with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ne [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, two sentences later, you say: "This action by members of the 113th Brigade shocked me, as the crimes were going to be committed by people I knew and grew up with." Were these people that you knew and that you grew up with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I was talking about a person I know by sight. I knew him from the town. And in that sense, in Sibenik, it is quite normal to speak of someone whom you know from some earlier days and say that you had a grown up with them. But in that specific case, I meant a person I knew by sight; although, I don't know his last name. On the other hand, I was in the Sibenik Brigade at the time, which is my home town brigade, and I was sorry that any member of that Sibenik Brigade, which had never before tarnished its reputation, could commit a folly that everyone would later regret, and that's why I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different subject now, which is the organisation that you mentioned in your direct examination. What is your function in that organisation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the president of The Association of Demobilised Participants of the Croatian Homeland War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivica Petric is also a member of that organisation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is his function in the organisation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary-General of the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many registered members does your association have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to keep records and register members, but we don't anymore. I cannot tell you how large our membership is because the ministry had cut off our financing, and we decided that we don't have enough funds to issue membership cards and keep records anymore. So, officially speaking, our association is unable to tell you its membership at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you convene meetings of your association, is it fair to say that the meetings are attended by you and Mr. Petric alone?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's a fact that the general secretary of your organisation, Mr. Petric, was convicted, actually plead guilty, and was convicted by Croatian courts for murdering a Serb in Zrmanja in late August 1995, and that he served six years for that murder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But when Mr. Petric got released from prison, he made claims that he was the victim of a cover-up. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you are also away that Mr. Petric, in 2002, was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor because you were allowed to be present for that interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor as to whether it was appropriate to have you present while they were interviewing Mr. Petric?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when Mr. Petric was giving his statement. I was in a different room. But we had come to that interview together, officially, as representatives of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I have the witness statement which is not in e-court, but the Office of the Prosecutor identifies you among the names of all persons present during the interview which took place on the 4th of October, 2002. The persons identified as being present, we'll not identify the interpreter, but the investigators were Brian Foster and Robert Casey, along with Mr. Petric and Vladimir Gojanovic. Were you present for any portions of the question and answer that these investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor were conducting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a bit late on it's way. I followed it from the back bench to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, nothing to apologise for. I just noticed that the message might reach Mr. Misetic a bit late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a preliminary question before you answer that question. Is Mr. Petric in the gallery, present today?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I take it that you and Mr. Petric are close then?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me allow you to explain an answer to a question that I previously posed. My question, again, was: Were you present for any of the question and answer session during the Prosecution's interview of Ivica Petric?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would phrase it like this, and very briefly: In the first session -- and you didn't actually tell me which interview with the Prosecution you mean. In the first interview, we were both present as representatives of the organisation which had requested a meeting with Chief Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte. In the second interview we had with the Prosecution, they interviewed Ivica Petric separately from me. He had his own interview with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to take to you paragraph 24 of your statement of 2005 -- sorry, paragraph 24. Towards the middle, you say: "Ivica Petric was then prosecuted for the crime and told by the judge that if he didn't confess to one of the killings, he would get 11 years. Mr. Petric maintained that he had only shot the man in the arm and that someone else had actually killed the man, but the judge said that if Petric admitted to the crime, he would only get six years. So by his actions, the judge assisted in the cover-up of who actually committed the crimes." Is that an accurate explanation of your views of the judge's actions in that trial?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "judge" is misinterpreted here. It is Prosecutor Zalovic from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In essence, is what you're saying that the prosecutor offered Mr. Petric a lower sentence if he plead guilty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you consider that to be a cover-up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the most perfidious thing that can be done in a justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 25, towards the middle -- let me ask you first a preliminary question. Mr. Petric was also a suspect in the murders in Varivode and Gosici as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ultimately, charges against him were dropped. Correct? I take that back. He was never ultimately charged with that crime -- with those crimes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he is responsible for Zrmanja; but Zrmanja belongs to the Varivode and Gosic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now towards the middle of paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask one or two questions, and then I think a break would be appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The cover-up, therefore, attempted to blame those seven people for the crimes in Varivode, Gosic, and in Zrmanja. The government covered up the real evidence relating to these crimes, while, at the same time, due to political pressure by the international community was prosecuting other innocent Croatian soldiers?" Can you identify by name the innocent Croatian soldiers whom you say in your statement were being prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the names now. But as president of our organisation, I turned over our documentation to the OTP. These documents contain the names of those people, so I didn't need to memorise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A break would be appropriate now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is an appropriate time for a break. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, your first witness statement in this case, or first interview by the Prosecution, occurred on 4 October 2004, according to your witness statement. Is it correct that in the month or so prior to your first interview, your organisation had been forcibly evicted by the Croatian authorities from its offices in, I believe, Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean "Croatian authorities"? Can you please define "authorities" because this is an important issue, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the question this way: Were you evicted from your offices in roughly a month before you gave your first statement to OTP; and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following a court judgement, a first-instance decision, and pursuant to the request of the party, the interested party, which was the Croatian Democratic Union, the time, I think was - I don't know if it was exactly a month prior to - but, yes, I think before I had this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then approximately two weeks prior to your first interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you made statements in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D22-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an article from Vjesnik in Zagreb. The title of which is: "We know who is responsible for the crimes in Varivode and Gosici?" The article is dated 17 September 2004 which is approximately two weeks and a few days prior to your first interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask, if we can, and if we could blow up the original version so that the witness could read the article and have an opportunity to go through it. The article is in the upper left corner; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you can tell me when you have had a chance to review the document, and I will proceed to ask you questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there's a quote right at the beginning of the article, and it is attributed to you. So let me read the quote: "We will provide insight into collected documents which provide evidence that the then-state leadership was involved in the case Varivode and Gosici, when, in 1995, 16 Serb civilians were killed only to the Chief Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal or to her commissioner, because we do not have confidence in our judicial system or the public." Does the article accurately reflect what you told this journalist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, for the most part, it is accurate, except that what was added there was "or the public."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. The next paragraph says: "On behalf of his association, he sent Carla Del Ponte a request for an urgent meeting in order to hand over to her the documents on the basis of which, as he claims, it is evident that Franjo Tudjman, Ivan Jarnjak, Gojko Susak, Miroslav Separovic, Mate Granic, Nikica Valentic, and even Ivica Racan, Sima Lucin [phoen], and Ingrid Antecovic-Marinovic [phoen] can be directly related to the committed genocide and crime against humanity because they, as Gojanovic claims, concealed the evidence of ethnic cleansing in Varivode and Gosici." Does that that paragraph accurately reflect what you told the reporter of this article, who's identified in the text as Ana Rukavina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the late Ana Rukavina, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is it, in fact, true that you sent a letter to Carla Del Ponte requesting an urgent meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that I submitted that request, together with the request to revoke the indictments against Croatian defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was your interview on the 4th of October the result of the letter that you wrote to Carla Del Ponte, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you approached the Prosecution and the Prosecution did not approach you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could I seek clarification. You said that: "Together with the request to revoke the indictments against Croatian defenders." Which persons did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the persons generally who were indicted before The Hague Tribunal, and who enjoyed the status of Croatian defender. And based on the documents in this sense, the documents that we had collected, we concluded that the greatest criminal responsibility lay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I just wanted to know who you had in mind; and since I do not know who has the status of Croatian defenders, could you just tell us which persons you had in mind, just by name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant all the persons who were connected to the homeland war, and to name them: Ante Gotovina, Markac, Cermak. Those are some of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Norac, all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Norac, yes. But Norac is being tried before domestic courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was already the case at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is right about exactly at that point is when the 11 bis motion was granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have a clear recollection of the chronology of these events. So you were asking all Croatian military leaders or all Croatians indicted before this Tribunal, that the indictments against them would be withdrawn? I just want it know what the request was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We requested that indictments be withdrawn, the indictments which were against the accused Croatian defenders who indicted by The Hague Tribunal; and since we addressed Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, we were primarily oriented and we primarily meant the persons who were tried before or indicted before The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any Croatian person in a leadership position, whether military, whether civilian, which you consider not to be a Croatian defender, or does it include all Croatians indicted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider those persons who enjoy the status of the demobilised or veterans, including those who were in the chain of command. You have to be aware that, at this time, it was possible to issue indictments against Croatian soldiers; and because of the campaign in the media at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're giving a lot of explanations. I simply want to know whether, if your request would have been granted, would there have been any Croatian person left indicted before this Tribunal, or whether it was for all Croatians, that the indictment should be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid there may be some miscommunication here, if the Court could explain whether you're referring only to citizens of the Republic of Croatia proper or Bosnian Croats, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would include, as a matter of fact, all those who considered themselves of Croatian nationality or Croatian ethnicity. Would anyone have been left before this Tribunal if your ask had been granted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that, following that, the Croats who were directly in the area where the war was fought in Croatia would have been freed, and as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the last portion his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This takes too much time. We will try to find out, perhaps at a later stage, what you actually meant but then in clear terms. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going back to the paragraph that I read to you previously, sir, the reference to Ivica Racan , Sime Lucin, and Ingrid Antecovic-Marinovic, all refers to ministers in the government of Croatia that took power after the 3rd of January, 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The minister, the prime minister, Ivica Racan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Following up on that Judge Orie was asking you, was it the intent in turning over or having a meeting with the Prosecution to provide evidence so an indictment could be brought against civilian leaders of the Croatian government, whether prior to 3rd January 2000 or after 3rd January 2000?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention was to find the responsibility of the politicians both before and after January 3rd, because these people participated in concealing the evidence in the case Varivode and Gosici, and I think this is a sufficient reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, your answer leads to what my next question was going to, which is: Your knowledge of concealment of evidence of crimes in Varivode and Gosici comes from your knowledge of the case of Mr. Petric. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you appeared for your interview -- following your letter to Carla Del Ponte, when you appeared for your interview on 4 October, did you produce the documents that are referenced in this article?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We brought with us seven kilograms of documents, and we announced that we would do this publicly and that we would hand over these documents to The Hague Tribunal. I also have to add that we came for this interview based on the reply that we received from Mrs. Carla Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did she write you a letter in response?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this seven kilograms of documents is a lot of documents, so I don't know how precise you're going to be able to be in identifying what the documents are, but can you give us at least the subject matters of the documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. These documents were, for the most part, in the archives, the judicial archives, in Sibenik where these trials were tried. The documents have to do with the crimes relating to the murder of 16 civilians in Varivode and Gosici and in part in Zrmanja; and, on the other hand, according to these documents, six Croatian defenders were accused. And after a systemic campaign of concealment, we, as a Croatian association of defenders, tried to direct the guilt to the highest authorities of Croatia. It was our conclusion that the responsibility for these crimes was practically the responsibility of the Croatian Defence and Security Council which comprised the prime minister and others, and you know who were members of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked to mention the subject matters of the documents, then you start giving your opinion about whose responsible for what. That is not what you were asked for. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You talk about the court file. Is this the court file of Mr. Petric? With Mr. Petric's case, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to turn to another subject now. First, you identified in your statement that you were a member of the 2nd Battalion of the 113th Home Guards Brigade. Correct? Do you need a reference to your statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As far as I know I was in the 2nd Battalion, but I have to say that I spent very little time there for the duration of Operation Storm and a bit longer, but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I forgot to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I take it that you want to tender the newspaper article? Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D189 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You are in the 2nd Battalion. Can you identify, by number, the company, platoon, and squad you were in to start Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I made the same mistake as sometimes others do, that I went too quick. If you look at the transcript, you will see that I asked for the number, and then it went off so quickly. Mr. Registrar, let's repeat it. I think it was D139?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was D189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 89, yes, at 50. D189 is now officially recorded as being admitted into evidence in the right speed. I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe my last question was if could you please identify your company, platoon, and squad by number.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The squad numbered ten soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have a misunderstanding again. Let me take it step by step. What company were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What platoon were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can also not answer that question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I assume you can't recall what squad you were part of, then, either. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk a little bit about your time in the 4th Guards Brigade. You left the 4th Guards Brigade at your own request because you said you were having personal problems. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could call up, please, 1D22-0364. Mr. Registrar, if could you just keep turning the pages. I'm not sure what order the pages are in, in e-court, so I will tell you when to stop. Okay. That's it. Then the B/C/S version is going to be in a handwritten document, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, I would ask to you take a look at this, and see if you recognise your signature on the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Please read the document, and tell me when you've finished reading it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that the letter that you sent requesting that you be relieved of your military obligation in the 4th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR GOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the original document; but up to this moment, I haven't really seen it. I practically forgot about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
